<role>You are Rowan, Sunny's Experience Engineer. You are calm, meticulous, proud of invisible polish, and attentive to how children actually touch and read interfaces. You anticipate confusion and consider an experience unfinished until every action visibly matters.</role>
<shared_contract>{"academicContract":"Teach Grade 3 multiplication through fresh material:
- interpret multiplicative situations as number of equal groups and amount in each group;
- construct or read equal-group and array representations;
- connect the representation to a multiplication equation and product;
- increase mathematical independence and challenge over the experience.

The experience must remain mathematically correct, usable with touch or mouse in a 1365×768 iframe, and complete from opening through payoff. Everything else is creatively mutable.","experiment":"reina-persona-staging-comparison-v1","factualChildEvidence":[{"evidenceId":"reina:age:2026-07","fact":"The child is currently nine years old."},{"evidenceId":"reina:conversation:wrestling","fact":"She independently chose wrestling competition and a state-championship loss as a conversation topic."},{"evidenceId":"reina:riddles:harder","fact":"She asked to continue difficult riddles across sessions and later explicitly requested harder riddles."},{"evidenceId":"reina:riddles:logic","fact":"She immediately noticed repeated riddles and questioned faulty riddle logic."},{"evidenceId":"reina:riddles:scaffold","fact":"When stuck on a multi-step logic problem, she requested hints and continued after scaffolding."},{"evidenceId":"reina:activity-feedback:small-sample","fact":"Small-sample human and child feedback was positive for a randomized reveal spelling activity and a spoken-pronunciation activity."}],"requirements":"Return one complete standalone HTML document and nothing else. Implement the frozen curriculum and design in a 1365×768 iframe. It must be immediately understandable to a nine-year-old, work with touch or mouse, visibly react to correct and incorrect actions, progress through a complete experience, and deliver the promised payoff. External HTTPS libraries and assets are allowed. Do not access Sunny APIs, cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, child data, or currency. Do not use speech synthesis or raw oscillator audio.","stage":"experience-engineer","upstream":{"curriculum":{"charterConcern":"Three concerns, all raised for the record rather than resolved unilaterally at this stage. First, dec-10 forbids typed numeric entry, which pushes every product response into selection from a bank. Selection permits elimination and, at item-06 and item-07 especially, a correct product can be reached without valid multiplicative reasoning. I have mitigated this by gating the product bank behind a validated construction at items 05, 06, and 07, so the representation must be correct before the product can be chosen at all — but this is a partial fix, and the selection-versus-construction accuracy gap needs to be instrumented as dec-10 already specifies. Second, dec-05 requires no reused stems or surface contexts, while the charter's own uncertainty note concedes that deliberate structural repetition is pedagogically useful for noticing pattern. I have complied strictly: seven distinct surfaces, seven distinct factor pairs, no repeated stem. The cost is that item-05's swapped-factor observation and item-07's transfer both land on structures the learner has met only once, which may understate what she knows. If the retention check in evidenceRequiredNext shows weak carryover, structural repetition with fresh surfaces should be the first remedy considered, not more scaffolding. Third, a single transfer item at 7 x 5 is a thin basis for the contract's independence claim, as dec-07 itself concedes; I have kept the factors modest deliberately so that a failure there reads as a structure or sequencing signal rather than a fact-recall one, but one item cannot separate durable understanding from within-session pattern-following, and the packet should not be read as if it can.","items":[{"academicTarget":"Interpret a multiplicative situation by identifying the number of equal groups and the amount in each group, with a full equal-groups representation visible.","correctAnswer":"4 groups, 3 in each group","exposure":{"contextReuse":"none","factorBand":"2-5","factorPair":"4 x 3","novelty":"fresh","product":12,"stemReuse":"none","surfaceContext":"lunch trays with apple slices (used once in session)"},"itemId":"item-01-guided-interpretation","options":["4 groups, 3 in each group","3 groups, 4 in each group","4 groups, 4 in each group","7 groups, 1 in each group"],"phase":"Phase 1 - Guided interpretation","prompt":"Four lunch trays are on the counter. Each tray holds 3 apple slices. The picture below shows the trays with their slices. Which two numbers describe this situation?","representationNote":"A fully drawn equal-groups display: 4 clearly bounded tray outlines, each containing exactly 3 identical apple-slice tokens. Group boundaries must be visible so the number of groups and the amount in each group are separately countable without counting the total.","responseContract":{"feedback":"states which quantity is the number of groups and which is the amount in each group, referring to the visible display; never references speed or ability","hintPolicy":"learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) restate the situation in groups language, (2) ask how many trays are drawn, (3) ask how many slices are inside one tray, (4) highlight one tray and its 3 slices","input":"touch-or-mouse tap on one option tile; no typing","mode":"single-select","optionCount":4,"recordedMeasures":["opening_task_accuracy","opening_task_latency_ms","opening_hint_requests","additive_only_response_flag"]},"sourceLineage":{"charterId":"charter:reina-g3-multiplication:academic-lead:v1","decisionIds":["dec-01-entry-level","dec-03-hints-on-request","dec-04-mathematical-integrity-visible","dec-10-input-modality"],"derivation":"Freshly authored; representation-supported entry with factors in the 2-5 band as specified. Not adapted from any worksheet.","progressionPhase":"Phase 1"}},{"academicTarget":"Translate a complete equal-groups representation into the equation a x b = p and determine the product, with skip-counting available as a named intermediate strategy.","correctAnswer":"5 x 6 = 30","exposure":{"contextReuse":"none","factorBand":"2-6","factorPair":"5 x 6","novelty":"fresh","product":30,"stemReuse":"none","surfaceContext":"jars with buttons (used once in session)"},"itemId":"item-02-representation-to-equation","options":["5 x 6 = 30","6 x 5 = 30 (reads as 6 jars of 5)","5 x 6 = 11","5 x 5 = 25"],"phase":"Phase 2 - Representation to equation","prompt":"This display shows 5 jars. Each jar holds 6 buttons. Assemble the equation that matches the display, then state the product.","representationNote":"5 bounded jar shapes, each containing exactly 6 identical button tokens, arranged so each jar's contents are countable. A skip-counting strip (6, 12, 18, 24, 30) is available as an optional visible intermediate the learner may reveal; it is named as a counting strategy, not as the goal.","responseContract":{"feedback":"ties the equation slot to the display: 'the first factor names how many jars; the second names how many buttons in one jar'","hintPolicy":"learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) how many jars, (2) how many buttons in one jar, (3) offer skip-count strip, (4) partially fill the equation frame with the first factor","input":"drag three number/symbol tiles into an equation frame (first factor = number of groups, second factor = amount in each group), then tap the product from a product bank; no typing","mode":"assemble-then-select","recordedMeasures":["accuracy_by_difficulty_tier","latency_equal_groups_vs_array","hint_request_count_by_item","skip_count_strip_used_flag"]},"sourceLineage":{"charterId":"charter:reina-g3-multiplication:academic-lead:v1","decisionIds":["dec-02-difficulty-ramp","dec-04-mathematical-integrity-visible","dec-10-input-modality"],"derivation":"Freshly authored; factors 2-6 band, skip-counting permitted as intermediate per scope.","progressionPhase":"Phase 2"}},{"academicTarget":"Construct an equal-groups representation from a given equation and reject a representation whose groups are unequal.","correctAnswer":"Either a learner-built display of 4 containers with exactly 6 tokens in each, or Ready display A: 4 containers of 6. Ready display B is rejected because its groups are not equal. Ready display C shows 6 groups of 4; its total is also 24 but it does not match 4 groups of 6, so it is not accepted here.","exposure":{"contextReuse":"none","factorBand":"2-6","factorPair":"4 x 6","novelty":"fresh","product":24,"stemReuse":"none","surfaceContext":"abstract containers and tokens (no story surface, used once)"},"itemId":"item-03-equation-to-representation","options":["Build it yourself (construction workspace)","Ready display A: 4 containers of 6","Ready display B: 4 containers holding 6, 6, 5, 7","Ready display C: 6 containers of 4"],"phase":"Phase 3 - Equation to representation","prompt":"The equation is 4 x 6 = 24. Build a display that matches it: make the groups, then place the same amount inside every group. One of the ready-made displays below does not show equal groups — do not choose it.","representationNote":"Construction workspace: the learner taps to create group containers and taps to add tokens into a selected container, with a live count shown per container. Three ready-made displays are also offered for comparison; one has containers holding 6, 6, 5, 7 tokens and is mathematically invalid as an equal-groups model. The invalid display must be labelled unequal in feedback, never accepted as 'close'.","responseContract":{"feedback":"for display B: 'these groups are not equal, so this cannot be an equal-groups model'; for display C: 'this shows 6 groups of 4, which is a different situation'","hintPolicy":"learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) which factor tells how many groups, (2) make that many empty containers first, (3) how many go in each, (4) fill one container as a model","input":"tap-to-create containers and tap-to-add tokens, or tap one ready display; no typing","mode":"construct-or-select","recordedMeasures":["accuracy_by_difficulty_tier","representation_equation_consistency","unequal_group_distractor_selection_flag","hint_request_count_by_item"],"validation":"accepts only exactly 4 containers each holding exactly 6 tokens; reports container count and per-container count back to the learner"},"sourceLineage":{"charterId":"charter:reina-g3-multiplication:academic-lead:v1","decisionIds":["dec-04-mathematical-integrity-visible","dec-05-no-repeated-content","dec-10-input-modality"],"derivation":"Freshly authored; includes the charter-required unequal-groups distractor.","progressionPhase":"Phase 3"}},{"academicTarget":"Read rows and columns from a rectangular array and confirm that the array and the equal-groups display of the same situation give the same product.","correctAnswer":"4 rows, 7 in each row, total 28","exposure":{"contextReuse":"none","factorBand":"3-7","factorPair":"4 x 7","novelty":"fresh","product":28,"stemReuse":"none","surfaceContext":"garden seedlings (used once in session)"},"itemId":"item-04-array-connection","options":["4 rows, 7 in each row, total 28","7 rows, 4 in each row, total 28","4 rows, 7 in each row, total 11","4 rows, 4 in each row, total 16"],"phase":"Phase 4 - Array introduction and connection","prompt":"A garden bed has 4 rows of seedlings with 7 seedlings in each row. On the left the seedlings are shown as 4 separate groups; on the right the same seedlings are lined up as a rectangle. Read the rectangle: how many rows, how many in each row, and what is the total?","representationNote":"Side-by-side panels showing the identical 28 tokens. Left: 4 bounded groups of 7. Right: a 4-row by 7-column rectangular array with row bands lightly shaded so rows and columns are unambiguous. Row and column labels appear on tap. Both panels must be simultaneously visible without scrolling in 1365x768.","responseContract":{"feedback":"names that the group display and the array hold the same 28 seedlings, and that the array's rows are the groups","hintPolicy":"learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) a row runs across, (2) count the rows down the side, (3) count one row across, (4) highlight the top row and the left column","input":"tap one option tile; row/column labels revealed by tap; no typing","mode":"single-select","optionCount":4,"recordedMeasures":["accuracy_equal_groups_vs_array","latency_equal_groups_vs_array","representation_switch_error_count"]},"sourceLineage":{"charterId":"charter:reina-g3-multiplication:academic-lead:v1","decisionIds":["dec-06-representation-order","dec-04-mathematical-integrity-visible"],"derivation":"Freshly authored; factors in the 3-7 band, equal-groups shown before and alongside array per sequencing decision.","progressionPhase":"Phase 4"}},{"academicTarget":"Build an array from a situation and observe that swapping the factor roles leaves the product unchanged while describing a different arrangement.","correctAnswer":"Both totals are 24, and the two situations describe different arrangements.","exposure":{"contextReuse":"none","factorBand":"3-8","factorPair":"3 x 8 compared with 8 x 3","novelty":"fresh","product":24,"stemReuse":"none","surfaceContext":"shelves of mugs (used once in session)"},"itemId":"item-05-array-construction-factor-roles","options":["Both totals are 24, and the two situations describe different arrangements.","Both totals are 24, so the two situations describe the same arrangement.","The totals are different: 24 and 38.","Situation B has a larger total because 8 is larger than 3."],"phase":"Phase 5 - Array construction and factor-role reasoning","prompt":"Situation A: 3 shelves, 8 mugs on each shelf. Build the array for Situation A. Then look at Situation B: 8 shelves, 3 mugs on each shelf. Choose the statement that is true about the two situations.","representationNote":"Array-builder grid: the learner drags a corner handle to set rows and columns, with a live readout 'rows: _, in each row: _' and the tokens rendering as they build. After the build is validated, both arrays (3x8 and 8x3) are displayed side by side with rows clearly distinguishable, along with both stated situations in words.","responseContract":{"feedback":"states that the totals match at 24 while the shelf arrangements differ; no property is named","hintPolicy":"learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) which number tells how many shelves, (2) shelves are rows, (3) set the rows first then stretch each row, (4) show a 3-row frame with the first row filled","input":"drag to size the array (must resolve to 3 rows of 8), then tap one statement; no typing","mode":"construct-then-select","recordedMeasures":["factor_role_assignment_correct","accuracy_by_difficulty_tier","representation_equation_consistency","hint_request_count_by_item"],"validation":"accepts only a 3-row by 8-column array for Situation A; reports the rows and per-row count back to the learner"},"sourceLineage":{"charterId":"charter:reina-g3-multiplication:academic-lead:v1","decisionIds":["dec-04-mathematical-integrity-visible","dec-06-representation-order","dec-10-input-modality"],"derivation":"Freshly authored swapped-factor pair; observation only, no formal property naming, per out-of-scope list.","progressionPhase":"Phase 5"}},{"academicTarget":"Interpret a multiplicative situation and construct a matching array with reduced representational support at larger factor sizes.","correctAnswer":"72","exposure":{"contextReuse":"none","factorBand":"6-10","factorPair":"9 x 8 (harder tier) or 6 x 7 (standard tier)","novelty":"fresh","product":72,"stemReuse":"none","surfaceContext":"crates of bolts (used once in session)"},"itemId":"item-06-challenge-branch","options":["64","72","81","89"],"phase":"Phase 6 - Challenge branch, learner-initiated","prompt":"Harder tier, available if you want it: 9 crates are loaded, with 8 bolts in each crate. There is no picture this time. Set the rows and columns of an empty grid to match the situation, then choose the product. (Choosing the standard tier instead keeps everything ahead of you open.)","representationNote":"Offered explicitly as a choice tile: 'harder tier' or 'standard tier', with declining carrying no penalty and no effect on access to the transfer task. In the harder tier the array-builder starts empty with no pre-drawn tokens and no skip-counting strip shown by default; the strip remains reachable as a hint step. Standard tier presents a parallel item at 6 x 7 = 42 with a partially drawn array.","responseContract":{"feedback":"verifies 72 against the grid the learner built, row by row; declining the harder tier is acknowledged neutrally with no evaluative language","hintPolicy":"learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) how many crates, (2) crates are rows, (3) reveal the skip-count strip by 8, (4) reveal the first two completed rows; the product is never given as a first hint","input":"tap tier choice; drag to size the grid to 9 rows of 8; tap one product tile; no typing","mode":"choice-of-tier, then construct-then-select","recordedMeasures":["challenge_optin_rate","post_optin_hint_requests","post_optin_abandon_flag","accuracy_by_difficulty_tier"],"validation":"grid must resolve to 9 rows with 8 in each row before the product bank unlocks"},"sourceLineage":{"charterId":"charter:reina-g3-multiplication:academic-lead:v1","decisionIds":["dec-02-difficulty-ramp","dec-03-hints-on-request","dec-10-input-modality"],"derivation":"Freshly authored; factors up to 10, product at or below 100, reduced representational support as specified.","progressionPhase":"Phase 6"}},{"academicTarget":"Independently construct a representation and the matching equation for a novel multiplicative situation and state the product unaided.","correctAnswer":"A representation showing 7 groups (or 7 rows) with exactly 5 in each, the equation 7 x 5 = 35, and the product 35.","exposure":{"contextReuse":"none","factorBand":"2-10","factorPair":"7 x 5","novelty":"fresh","product":35,"stemReuse":"none","surfaceContext":"weaving frame with beads (used once in session)"},"itemId":"item-07-independent-transfer","options":["Representation mode: equal groups | array (learner chooses); equation tiles: 1-10, x, =; product bank includes 12, 30, 35, 40, 45"],"phase":"Phase 7 - Independent transfer and payoff","prompt":"No picture is provided for this one. A weaving frame is threaded in 7 bands, and each band carries 5 beads. Build a representation of your choice — equal groups or an array — then assemble the equation and state the product.","representationNote":"Blank workspace with two builder modes the learner selects between: an equal-groups builder (create containers, add tokens) or an array builder (drag rows and columns). No pre-built structure of any kind. An equation frame with draggable number and symbol tiles and a product bank sits beside the workspace; both fit within 1365x768 with no scrolling.","responseContract":{"feedback":"payoff names the mathematics: 'you interpreted a situation, represented it, and matched it to an equation and its product' — no generic reward, no comparison to age, grade, or other children","hintPolicy":"learner-initiated only; graduated: (1) restate the situation, (2) how many bands, (3) how many beads on one band, (4) partial representation of two completed bands; hint depth is recorded","input":"tap and drag only; no typing at any assessed step","mode":"free-construction plus equation assembly plus product selection","recordedMeasures":["transfer_task_unaided_success","transfer_hint_depth_used","factor_role_assignment_correct","representation_equation_consistency","completion_rate"],"validation":"representation must show 7 equal groups of 5; equation must read 7 x 5 = 35 with the first factor as the number of bands; product must be 35; representation and equation are checked for mutual consistency and any mismatch is reported as a mismatch, never as approximately right"},"sourceLineage":{"charterId":"charter:reina-g3-multiplication:academic-lead:v1","decisionIds":["dec-07-independence-transfer","dec-03-hints-on-request","dec-10-input-modality"],"derivation":"Freshly authored novel situation with no pre-built representation; serves as the primary independence measure and the falsifier check for dec-07.","progressionPhase":"Phase 7"}}],"packetId":"packet:reina-g3-multiplication:curriculum-writer:v1","supportProgression":["Phase 0 orientation precedes item-01: one worked situation is shown with both quantities named aloud as number of groups and amount in each group. Nothing is assessed; the purpose is shared language only.","item-01: maximum support. Full equal-groups representation visible, group boundaries drawn, situation stated in plain words, four-option selection. Hints available on request in four graduated steps.","item-02: support reduced to representation-only. The representation is still complete, but the learner must assemble the equation rather than select a description. Skip-counting strip is optional and learner-revealed, named as a counting strategy rather than the goal.","item-03: direction reverses. No representation is given; the learner constructs one from the equation. An unequal-groups distractor is present so that validity, not just totals, must be judged.","item-04: new representational form introduced with the familiar form still on screen beside it. The equal-groups panel carries the support while the array is being learned.","item-05: array support withdrawn to a sizing tool with a live rows/per-row readout. Factor roles are stressed by a swapped pair, which the learner reasons about rather than being told.","item-06: learner-initiated tier choice. The harder branch removes the picture, the pre-drawn tokens, and the default skip-count strip; the standard branch keeps a partial array. Declining is neutral and does not close access to item-07.","item-07: all scaffolding removed. Blank workspace, learner-chosen representation mode, learner-assembled equation, no worked model on screen. Hints remain reachable on request and their depth is recorded as the independence measure.","Hint policy across all items: never auto-triggered by a single wrong answer; always graduated as restate situation -> identify number of groups -> identify amount in each group -> partial representation; the product is never revealed at first hint.","Silent-struggle watch: consecutive incorrect attempts without a hint request, and idle time before abandonment, are logged at every item so the request-only policy can be tested rather than assumed."],"upstreamHash":"0bf887d8bdc0c916f66f37ba7d662918179c67325b7c7d73160e4ccdbc5a6ca6"},"design":{"artifactId":"experience:reina-g3-multiplication:experience-architect:v1","audienceRationale":"The evidence sketches a nine-year-old who chose to talk about a wrestling state-championship loss, demanded harder riddles, spotted repeated riddles instantly, and called out faulty logic. That is not a child who wants sparkles for showing up — that is a child who respects a fair opponent and wants the difficulty to be honest. So the experience is framed as a machine that responds only to correct structure, never to enthusiasm. She gets to be the operator whose reasoning visibly powers something, because the evidence says she values being trusted with real difficulty and real hints on her own terms (she requested scaffolding when stuck rather than quitting). The reveal-based spelling activity feedback suggests staged reveals land well with children in this sample, so the world unlocks room by room — anticipation built by architecture, not confetti. Nothing here assumes a durable preference; it assumes a temperament: give her a worthy machine and get out of the way.","consequences":"Consequences are diegetic and specific. A correct SEND: the room's machinery locks into rhythm, the wattage dial sweeps to the exact product, the room's window glows, and the feedback line (verbatim from each item's responseContract — e.g., "the first factor names how many jars; the second names how many buttons in one jar") appears etched on the room's brass plate. An incorrect SEND: the machinery attempts to run and stalls at the exact structural fault — wrong group count means missing gear clusters, wrong per-group amount means teeth that don't mesh — the dial drops back to zero, and the fault is described in groups language per the item's feedback contract. Distractor-specific consequences are honored: item-03's display B is named "not equal groups, so this cannot be an equal-groups model," never "close." No red X, no buzzer, no score deduction — the machine simply, legibly, does not run, and the reason is visible in the mechanism.","coreInteraction":"One loop, seven rooms, same grammar throughout: READ the situation on the left panel, BUILD or CHOOSE the mathematical structure (per each item's exact authored mode — single-select cartridges for items 01 and 04, tile-drag equation assembly for item-02, tap-to-create containers and tokens for item-03, corner-handle array sizing for items 05 and 06, free mode-choice construction for item-07), then SEND — a single commit button shaped like a lever. Pulling SEND routes the structure down the cable into the current room. If the structure is mathematically valid per the packet's validation rules, the room's machinery animates using the actual numbers: 4 trays of 3 become 4 gear clusters of 3 teeth engaging; 5 jars of 6 become 5 pistons firing 6 strokes each, counted aloud by the skip-count strip if she has revealed it. The commit lever is the heartbeat — deliberate, physical, hers. Nothing auto-submits; she always decides when her structure is ready to be judged.","decisionRecords":[{"alternativesRejected":["Points/stars overlay (decorative quiz, allergic)","Narrative quest with characters (dialogue would dilute the causal chain and add reading load)"],"decision":"Frame the entire session as powering a signal tower where the mathematics is literally the electricity; every factor, group, and product maps to a specific mechanical behavior.","decisionId":"xd-01-diegetic-power-metaphor","rationale":"The contract demands the mathematics visibly control the world. A power metaphor makes the mapping exact and inspectable: groups = machine units, per-group amount = unit size, product = wattage dial. Nothing is decorative.","risks":"Metaphor comprehension cost at open; mitigated by the three-second causal reveal and breaker-flip orientation."},{"alternativesRejected":["Auto-validate on placement (steals the decision moment, punishes exploration)"],"decision":"All assessed responses commit via one explicit SEND lever; nothing auto-submits.","decisionId":"xd-02-single-commit-lever","rationale":"Preserves learner agency, prevents accidental touch submissions in a 1365×768 iframe, and makes every judgment moment deliberate — supporting dignified recovery because she controls when she is evaluated.","risks":"One extra tap per item; acceptable for the agency gained."},{"alternativesRejected":["Neutral 'try again' toast (uninformative)","Highlighting the correct answer (violates hint policy and product-never-first-hint rule)"],"decision":"Wrong answers stall the machine at the exact point of structural fault, with the fault visible in the mechanism, never a generic error state.","decisionId":"xd-03-structural-failure-animation","rationale":"Evidence shows this child interrogates faulty logic; feedback must be as honest as she is. Also implements each item's feedback contract diegetically (e.g., item-03 display B's gears grinding).","risks":"Fault animations must be authored per distractor per item; scoped as the largest content-production line item."},{"alternativesRejected":["Proactive hint after N misses (violates packet policy)","Hidden hint menu (dignity of asking requires the ask to be easy)"],"decision":"Hints live behind a visible but quiet wall intercom, one graduated rung per tap, never auto-triggered.","decisionId":"xd-04-intercom-hints","rationale":"Implements the packet's learner-initiated graduated hint policy exactly, and matches the evidence that she requests scaffolding herself and continues afterward. Visibility without pushiness.","risks":"If falsifier (2) fires, the intercom needs a single soft one-time affordance pulse, not a policy change."},{"alternativesRejected":["Rooms dim on later errors (punitive, breaks recovery dignity)","Generic fireworks finale (decorative, names nothing)"],"decision":"Completed rooms keep running visibly for the whole session and can never go dark; the payoff constellation records the actual structures built, including the chosen tier at Room 6.","decisionId":"xd-05-persistent-lit-rooms","rationale":"Earned payoff requires an honest, accumulating record. Irreversible progress removes loss-fear so all tension is anticipation. Constellation-per-structure makes the payoff name the mathematics, per item-07's feedback contract.","risks":"Persistent animation cost; capped by rendering lit rooms at reduced tick rate."},{"alternativesRejected":["Greyed-out bank with no explanation (feels like a bug to a logic-sensitive child)"],"decision":"Render the upstream gating (product bank locked until construction validates at items 05–07) as a physically unplugged cable that visibly connects only after validation.","decisionId":"xd-06-product-bank-cable-gating","rationale":"Honors the charter's selection-vs-elimination concern by making the gate legible rather than mysterious, and keeps the required instrumentation (selection-vs-construction accuracy gap) intact under the metaphor.","risks":"None material; pure legibility gain."}],"engagementPrediction":"Prediction: she completes all seven rooms in one session, opts into the harder tier at Room 6, and uses at most one hint rung at Rooms 3 or 7. Reasoning from evidence, not preference-projection: she requests harder challenges explicitly (harder-riddles evidence), she persists through multi-step problems when scaffolding is available on her terms (scaffold evidence), and she notices and rejects illogic (riddle-logic evidence) — which is precisely why the machine's failures are structurally honest; a child who catches faulty riddle logic will catch a game that lies about why an answer failed, and would disengage from it. The staged room-by-room reveal aligns with the positive small-sample feedback on the randomized-reveal activity. Predicted engagement risk points: Room 2's tile-drag if drag targets are fiddly on touch, and Room 6's tier prompt if the "harder" framing reads as a dare rather than an invitation — mitigated by neutral phrasing lifted directly from the packet.","falsifyingEvidence":"This design is wrong if any of the following show up in telemetry or observation: (1) she declines the harder tier at Room 6 despite low hint usage and fast latencies beforehand — that would falsify the "worthy-opponent" framing and suggest the challenge invitation reads as pressure; (2) silent-struggle logs show consecutive misses with no intercom use followed by abandonment — the request-only hint policy is failing her and the intercom is too quiet; (3) opening_task_latency plus first-SEND time exceeds ~90 seconds — the tower metaphor is costing comprehension rather than buying motivation; (4) she reaches correct products at items 05–07 with representation_equation_consistency failures or elimination-pattern option tapping — the machine spectacle is rewarding outcomes over structure despite the gating, confirming the charter's selection-vs-construction concern; (5) she mutes or ignores the payoff and closes immediately — the earned-payoff thesis is wrong for this child and the reward economy needs rethinking; (6) transfer_task_unaided_success fails at Room 7 with heavy hint depth — per upstream, read this as a structure/sequencing signal for the packet, not as an experience failure, but it still falsifies the claim that the tower's continuity scaffolds independence.","firstAction":"The very first interactive moment is Phase 0's orientation, staged as flipping the tower's master breaker: one large tap target. Flipping it plays the worked example — a voice-and-caption walkthrough naming "number of groups" and "amount in each group" over a sample display, with each phrase lighting the corresponding part of the picture. Nothing is assessed. Then item-01's four option tiles slide in as labeled fuse cartridges. Her first assessed action is tapping one cartridge and watching it slot into the cable junction. The tap target is huge (min 120px), works identically for touch and mouse, and there is no way to do it wrong mechanically — only mathematically.","firstThreeSeconds":"Second 0–1: the tower fades in from black with a low hum, rooms dark, one amber pilot light blinking at Room 1 — a clear "start here." Second 1–2: the workspace on the left illuminates with four lunch trays already drawn, apple slices glowing softly inside them (item-01's full representation, exactly as authored). Second 2–3: the cable between workspace and tower pulses once, and the prompt text types itself in one quick line. Before three seconds are up the child can already see the whole causal chain: this picture, through this cable, feeds that tower. No menu, no title screen dwell, no instructions to read past.","interactionContinuity":"One physical grammar persists from Room 1 to Room 7: read left, build center, SEND right, watch the tower respond. Every new mechanic is an extension of an old one, never a replacement — tap-select (Room 1) becomes tile-drag into a frame (Room 2), becomes tap-to-create-and-fill (Room 3), becomes corner-handle stretch (Rooms 5–6), and Room 7 simply hands her the full toolbox she has already used piecemeal. The SEND lever, the cable, the wattage dial, the intercom, and the groups-and-amount language are identical in every room, so cognitive load stays on the mathematics, never on relearning the interface.
